summary: This document updates RFC 7252 and changes the registration procedures for the CoAP Content-Formats IANA registry. It adds a Media Type column to that registry and also reserves some Content-Format identifiers.

eli5.summary: CoAP has a list of numbers that stand for kinds of data. This changes the rules for adding to the list and adds a column showing the matching media type name.

questions: how are coap content-format ids assigned
what is the coap content-formats registry
which coap content-format ids are reserved for documentation
what is the coap expert review checklist
subtitle: New rules for handing out CoAP Content-Format numbers, so bad registrations stop slipping through.

tldr.problem: The old rules for the CoAP Content-Formats registry did not require anyone to check that a requested Content-Type and Content Coding combination was valid, which has already led to erroneous registrations.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC replaces Section 12.3 of RFC 7252 with per-range registration rules, an Expert Review checklist, a preferred string format, temporary registrations and a new Media Type column.
tldr.outcome: Most of the identifier space now gets a designated-expert check, and 64998 and 64999 are reserved for documentation.

today: RFC 9876 is a Proposed Standard published in November 2025. It updates RFC 7252 and no later RFC is recorded as updating or obsoleting it.

sections.title: Why the Registry Rules Changed
sections.content:
RFC 7252 set up the CoAP Content-Formats registry. It gave rules for the "IETF Review or IESG Approval" range (256-9999) and the "First Come First Served" (FCFS) range (10000-64999). In the FCFS range the designated expert was not involved, and IANA staff alone finished the registration.

The rules did not explicitly require checking that the combination of Content-Type (a Media Type with optional parameters) and Content Coding was semantically valid. That check is generally non-trivial and should not be left only to the registrar. The RFC says this gap may confuse both sides and has already led to erroneous registrations.

This document updates RFC 7252 to reduce the risk of unintentional or malicious errors. It amends the ranges, adds a review procedure for most of them, and allows temporary identifiers.
sections.eli5: Imagine a club list where the helper who wrote names down never checked if a name made sense. Some wrong names got in, so now there is a proper checker.

sections.title: Registry Ranges and Policies
sections.content:
Section 4.1 replaces Section 12.3 of RFC 7252. Each registry entry holds the Content Type, the Content Coding (if any), the Media Type registered with IANA, a numeric identifier in the range 0-65535, and a reference to a document describing what the payload means. CoAP has no separate way to carry a Content Coding, so the coding is part of each identifier. If several codings are used with one Media Type, each gets its own identifier.

  • 0-255: Expert Review, because the single-byte space is so small.
  • 256-9999: IETF Review with Expert Review, or IESG Approval with Expert Review.
  • 10000-19999 and 33000-64997: Expert Review.
  • 20000-32999: First Come First Served, with limits.
  • 64998-64999: reserved for documentation.
  • 65000-65535: experimental use. These MUST NOT be used in operational deployments.

An FCFS request must consist solely of a registered Media Type name, with no parameter names and no Content Coding, and the Media Type must not already be used in the registry. If that does not fit, the requester can ask for a different range that needs Expert Review. For the 256-9999 range, the early allocation procedure of RFC 7120 also applies.
sections.eli5: The list is split into zones. Some zones need a careful grown-up to approve, one zone is first come first served for simple things, and the last zone is only for experiments.

sections.title: The Expert Review Checklist
sections.content:
The designated expert works through a five-point checklist:

  1. The Content-Type and Content Coding combination must not already be in the registry.
  2. The Media Type must be registered in the "Media Types" registry or approved for registration. It may instead be in the "Provisional Standard Media Type Registry", but provisional types are only allowed in the ranges 0-255 and 256-9999.
  3. Any optional parameter names must be defined for that Media Type, and parameter values must be permitted.
  4. The Content Type must be in the preferred format.
  5. Any Content Coding must exist, or be approved, in the "HTTP Content Coding Registry".

For the 0-255 range the expert also weighs the scarcity of 1-byte code points. A similar concern may apply in other ranges when parameters and codings consume considerable code point space.

The preferred format follows Section 8.3.1 of RFC 9110: lowercase for case-insensitive elements, parameter values quoted only when a quoted-string is required, and a single semicolon with no adjacent whitespace between the Media Type and parameters. The expert or IANA may rewrite a request into this form before approval.
sections.eli5: The checker asks five questions. Is it new? Is the data type real? Are the extra settings real? Is it written neatly? Is the squishing method real?

sections.title: Examples of Invalid Requests
sections.content:
Section 4.1.5 gives sample requests that would have been approved under the old Section 12.3 of RFC 7252 but fail the new checklist. They use identifiers 64998 and 64999 and are meant to train the expert's eye. They are a representative sample, not an exhaustive one.

  • An unknown Media Type, such as application/unknown+cbor.
  • An unknown parameter, such as application/cose;unknown-parameter=1.
  • An invalid parameter value, such as application/cose;cose-type=invalid.
  • An unknown Content Coding, such as inflate with application/senml+cbor.
  • Duplicates in disguise: a parameter set to its default value, the default identity coding, or a URN whose case-insensitive namespace differs only in case (urn:example:1 versus urn:EXAMPLE:1).
sections.eli5: The RFC shows pretend forms with mistakes, like a made-up name or the same entry written twice in a sneaky way, so the checker knows what to catch.

sections.title: Temporary Registrations and the Media Type Column
sections.content:
The registry now allows temporary registrations within the 0-64997 range, for example through an IANA early allocation. A registration that refers to a provisional Media Type is always temporary. IANA marks it as temporary, and removes that mark once the required procedure completes and the Media Type is in the "Media Types" registry. If the procedure fails, or the provisional Media Type is abandoned, IANA removes the entry and sets the identifier back to "Unassigned". In the 10000-64997 range, an abandoned document does not cause removal, because that range needs no standards process or registering document.

Temporary registrations in the 0-255 range are exempt from the formal renewal process of RFC 7120. The designated experts direct IANA to remove them.

IANA has also added a Media Type column, placed to the right of the "Content Type" column. It lists the base Media Type name with a hyperlink to its IANA record, and requesters do not fill it in separately.
sections.eli5: Some entries can be written in pencil while they wait for approval. If approval never comes, the pencil entry is erased and the number goes back in the pile.

sections.title: Security and IANA Actions
sections.content:
The security section is short: the new procedures reduce the chances of malicious manipulation of the registry, and otherwise the Security Considerations of RFC 7252 are unchanged.

IANA has added a note that temporary registrations in the 0-255 range are approved by designated experts and are not subject to the RFC 7120 renewal process. IANA has also listed this document as an additional reference for the registry, and has reserved Content-Format identifiers 64998 and 64999 for use in documentation.
sections.eli5: A stricter checker makes it harder for anyone to sneak a bad entry onto the list. Two numbers are kept free for examples in guides.
